identity.title: Chest percussion hyperresonance (diffuse with barrel chest = COPD; unilateral = pneumothorax)

technique.how: With the patient sitting, percuss symmetric points over both lung fields anteriorly and posteriorly, comparing side to side; hyperresonance is a louder, lower-pitched, more drum-like note than normal resonance. Note whether it is bilateral (hyperinflation) or unilateral (air in the pleural space), and combine with breath-sound asymmetry.
technique.prerequisites: Quiet room, chest exposed, examiner able to compare with normal resonance.
technique.contraindications: None; avoid delaying decompression for percussion in a hypotensive patient with suspected tension pneumothorax.

interpretation.positive_finding: Bilateral hyperresonance in a smoker strongly raises the probability of COPD (LR+ about 9.5 in primary care); unilateral hyperresonance with reduced breath sounds points to pneumothorax on that side.
interpretation.negative_finding: Normal percussion note does not exclude COPD (sensitivity about 0.2) or a small pneumothorax; the sign is a rule-in, not a rule-out, finding.
interpretation.pitfalls: Obesity, a thick chest wall and examiner skill blunt the sign; interobserver agreement for percussion is poor. Large bullae or a contralateral effusion can mimic unilateral hyperresonance.
interpretation.changes_what: Bilateral: pursue spirometry/COPD; unilateral with breath-sound loss: obtain CXR or POCUS for pneumothorax now; normal: no change in probability.

estimates.population: 375 primary-care patients aged >=40 y with a previous diagnosis of asthma or COPD (cross-sectional, Norway)

estimates.target_condition: Severe COPD (post-bronchodilator spirometry threshold as defined in Table 4)
estimates.population: Same 375 primary-care patients aged >=40 y with previous asthma/COPD diagnosis
estimates.reference_standard: Post-bronchodilator spirometry (severe COPD definition per Table 4)

sources.citation: Oshaug K, Halvorsen PA, Melbye H. Should chest examination be reinstated in the early diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis. 2013.
Holleman DR, Simel DL. Does the clinical examination predict airflow limitation? JAMA. 1995.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use percussion to exclude pneumothorax in trauma or after a procedure; image instead.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Unilateral hyperresonance with absent breath sounds, hypotension or tracheal deviation = tension pneumothorax; decompress before imaging.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Oshaug 2013 (Discussion) states previous studies showed considerable interobserver variation, particularly for hyperresonance to percussion and diminished breath sounds; no kappa is given in the accessible text.

extraction_notes: Estimates are from Oshaug 2013 Tables 3-4 (PMC3751499); table columns read sensitivity, specificity, LR+, 95% CI, and a final column (86.1/47.2) that appears to be PPV or post-test probability - not entered. LR- is not tabulated. Prevalence figures quoted from table notes: 'The overall prevalence of COPD was 39.7%' (Table 3 note) and 'The overall prevalence of severe COPD was 11.7%' (Table 4 note); the exact FEV1 threshold for 'severe COPD' sits in the Table 4 caption which was truncated in the retrieved text. The 1995 JAMA RCE (PMID 7815660) has an empty abstract in e-utils and no open-access text, so its pooled hyperresonance values could not be quoted. No diagnostic-accuracy study of percussion for pneumothorax was found ('hyperresonance percussion pneumothorax sensitivity' returned nothing; 'physical examination pneumothorax diagnostic accuracy emergency' returned ultrasound papers only), so the pneumothorax use is guideline/teaching-based only.
